newsitem.title: GERMANY: German peace groups say army cuts can fix budget.
newsitem.headline: German peace groups say army cuts can fix budget.

text.p: Three German peace think-tanks proposed on Tuesday that beleaguered Finance Minister Theo Waigel make a billion mark ($583.6 million) budget cut by cutting the size of the army and abolishing conscription.
The end of the Cold War and the fact Germany was no longer a "front-line" nation meant the army could be cut from 340,000 to a professional force of 200,000, they concluded in a study.

Such a reduction would create savings of some 10 billion marks, according to the report by the University of Hamburg Peace Research Institute, the Hesse Foundation for Peace Research and the Evangelical Study Group.
A Defence Ministry spokesman said the government was committed to retaining army numbers at existing levels and to keeping the current mix of professional and conscripted soldiers.

Waigel needs at least 10-15 billion marks in spending cuts or additional revenue for Bonn to overcome a Maastricht Treaty hurdle limiting state deficits of nations who want to join the 1999 launch of Europe's planned single currency.

Thwarted in an attempt to create windfall profits by revaluing Bundesbank gold reserves, Waigel is scraping for alternatives. He recently announced a state spending freeze and plans for further privatisations and state cost-savings. ($ = 1.713 German Marks)
